title: Why Narration Is A Bad Classroom Management Strategy ment-strategy/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin critiques narration, the common practice of describing aloud the positive behaviors a teacher observes while students are mid-task. He explains its intended purposes as reminder, model, and incentive for imitation, then dismantles it as a disguised form of false praise. He argues narration ignores misbehavior, weakens listening skills because students learn the teacher will repeat directions, and diminishes in effectiveness over time as students tune it out. Most seriously, he contends it fosters dependence and signals to students that the teacher doubts their competence. The article ends by urging teachers to ask more of students, not less, and to let quality instruction stand on its own without a constant narrated soundtrack.
points: Narration is defined as describing students' positive behavior aloud while they are performing it, and Linsin argues it is really a form of false praise.
Narration is said to weaken listening skills because students learn directions will be repeated for them via narration.
It diminishes over time as students stop responding to being publicly named and described.
It fosters dependence and implicitly communicates that the teacher doesn't believe students can act without prompting.
The remedy is to give clear, detailed instruction up front and then step back, holding students responsible for carrying it out on their own.
quotes: Even though you’re merely expressing what you see, without judgement, make no mistake: Narration is a form of false praise .
If your students know you’re going to remind them of what they need to do through narration, then there is no reason to listen closely to your initial directions.

Narration effectively teaches students that they need you to talk them through even the simplest tasks. Thus, they struggle when asked to do anything on their own, especially more complex academic work.
Because narration inhibits the development of maturity and independence and creates a weak-minded, needy class. It creates learned helplessness and a fear of failure.

Viewed from a student’s perspective, the only reason their teacher would narrate them through a simple direction is if the teacher believes they can’t do it on their own—which is the main message they receive.
